title: Longest increasing subsequence
html:
We are given an array with nnn numbers: a[0…n−1]a[0 \dots n-1]a[0…n−1]. The task is to find the longest, strictly increasing, subsequence in aaa.

Formally we look for the longest sequence of indices i1,…iki_1, \dots i_ki1​,…ik​ such that

i1<i2<⋯<ik,a[i1]<a[i2]<⋯<a[ik]i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_k,\quad a[i_1] < a[i_2] < \dots < a[i_k]i1​<i2​<⋯<ik​,a[i1​]<a[i2​]<⋯<a[ik​]

In this article we discuss multiple algorithms for solving this task. Also we will discuss some other problems, that can be reduced to this problem.

Solution in O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) with dynamic programming {data-toc-label="Solution in O(n^2) with dynamic programming"}

Dynamic programming is a very general technique that allows to solve a huge class of problems. Here we apply the technique for our specific task.

First we will search only for the length of the longest increasing subsequence, and only later learn how to restore the subsequence itself.

Finding the length

To accomplish this task, we define an array d[0…n−1]d[0 \dots n-1]d[0…n−1], where d[i]d[i]d[i] is the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends in the element at index iii.

example

a={8,3,4,6,5,2,0,7,9,1}d={1,1,2,3,3,1,1,4,5,2}\begin{array}{ll} a &= \{8, 3, 4, 6, 5, 2, 0, 7, 9, 1\} \\ d &= \{1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 1, 1, 4, 5, 2\} \end{array}ad​={8,3,4,6,5,2,0,7,9,1}={1,1,2,3,3,1,1,4,5,2}​

The longest increasing subsequence that ends at index 4 is {3,4,5}\{3, 4, 5\}{3,4,5} with a length of 3, the longest ending at index 8 is either {3,4,5,7,9}\{3, 4, 5, 7, 9\}{3,4,5,7,9} or {3,4,6,7,9}\{3, 4, 6, 7, 9\}{3,4,6,7,9}, both having length 5, and the longest ending at index 9 is {0,1}\{0, 1\}{0,1} having length 2.

We will compute this array gradually: first d[0]d[0]d[0], then d[1]d[1]d[1], and so on. After this array is computed, the answer to the problem will be the maximum value in the array d[]d[]d[].

So let the current index be iii. I.e. we want to compute the value d[i]d[i]d[i] and all previous values d[0],…,d[i−1]d[0], \dots, d[i-1]d[0],…,d[i−1] are already known. Then there are two options:

  • d[i]=1d[i] = 1d[i]=1: the required subsequence consists only of the element a[i]a[i]a[i].

  • d[i]>1d[i] > 1d[i]>1: The subsequence will end at a[i]a[i]a[i], and right before it will be some number a[j]a[j]a[j] with j<ij < ij<i and a[j]<a[i]a[j] < a[i]a[j]<a[i].

    It's easy to see, that the subsequence ending in a[j]a[j]a[j] will itself be one of the longest increasing subsequences that ends in a[j]a[j]a[j]. The number a[i]a[i]a[i] just extends that longest increasing subsequence by one number.

    Therefore, we can just iterate over all j<ij < ij<i with a[j]<a[i]a[j] < a[i]a[j]<a[i], and take the longest sequence that we get by appending a[i]a[i]a[i] to the longest increasing subsequence ending in a[j]a[j]a[j]. The longest increasing subsequence ending in a[j]a[j]a[j] has length d[j]d[j]d[j], extending it by one gives the length d[j]+1d[j] + 1d[j]+1.

    d[i]=max⁡j<ia[j]<a[i](d[j]+1)d[i] = \max_{\substack{j < i \\\\ a[j] < a[i]}} \left(d[j] + 1\right)d[i]=j<ia[j]<a[i]​max​(d[j]+1)

If we combine these two cases we get the final answer for d[i]d[i]d[i]:

d[i]=max⁡(1,max⁡j<ia[j]<a[i](d[j]+1))d[i] = \max\left(1, \max_{\substack{j < i \\\\ a[j] < a[i]}} \left(d[j] + 1\right)\right)d[i]=max​1,j<ia[j]<a[i]​max​(d[j]+1)​

Implementation

Here is an implementation of the algorithm described above, which computes the length of the longest increasing subsequence.

int lis(vector<int> const& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    vector<int> d(n, 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
            if (a[j] < a[i])
                d[i] = max(d[i], d[j] + 1);
        }
    }

    int ans = d[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        ans = max(ans, d[i]);
    }
    return ans;
}

Restoring the subsequence

So far we only learned how to find the length of the subsequence, but not how to find the subsequence itself.

To be able to restore the subsequence we generate an additional auxiliary array p[0…n−1]p[0 \dots n-1]p[0…n−1] that we will compute alongside the array d[]d[]d[]. p[i]p[i]p[i] will be the index jjj of the second last element in the longest increasing subsequence ending in iii. In other words the index p[i]p[i]p[i] is the same index jjj at which the highest value d[i]d[i]d[i] was obtained. This auxiliary array p[]p[]p[] points in some sense to the ancestors.

Then to derive the subsequence, we just start at the index iii with the maximal d[i]d[i]d[i], and follow the ancestors until we deduced the entire subsequence, i.e. until we reach the element with d[i]=1d[i] = 1d[i]=1.

Implementation of restoring

We will change the code from the previous sections a little bit. We will compute the array p[]p[]p[] alongside d[]d[]d[], and afterwards compute the subsequence.

For convenience we originally assign the ancestors with p[i]=−1p[i] = -1p[i]=−1. For elements with d[i]=1d[i] = 1d[i]=1, the ancestors value will remain −1-1−1, which will be slightly more convenient for restoring the subsequence.

vector<int> lis(vector<int> const& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    vector<int> d(n, 1), p(n, -1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
            if (a[j] < a[i] && d[i] < d[j] + 1) {
                d[i] = d[j] + 1;
                p[i] = j;
            }
        }
    }

    int ans = d[0], pos = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (d[i] > ans) {
            ans = d[i];
            pos = i;
        }
    }

    vector<int> subseq;
    while (pos != -1) {
        subseq.push_back(a[pos]);
        pos = p[pos];
    }
    reverse(subseq.begin(), subseq.end());
    return subseq;
}

Alternative way of restoring the subsequence

It is also possible to restore the subsequence without the auxiliary array p[]p[]p[]. We can simply recalculate the current value of d[i]d[i]d[i] and also see how the maximum was reached.

This method leads to a slightly longer code, but in return we save some memory.

Solution in O(nlog⁡n)O(n \log n)O(nlogn) with dynamic programming and binary search {data-toc-label="Solution in O(n log n) with dynamic programming and binary search"}

In order to obtain a faster solution for the problem, we construct a different dynamic programming solution that runs in O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2), and then later improve it to O(nlog⁡n)O(n \log n)O(nlogn).

We will use the dynamic programming array d[0…n]d[0 \dots n]d[0…n]. This time d[l]d[l]d[l] doesn't correspond to the element a[i]a[i]a[i] or to a prefix of the array. d[l]d[l]d[l] will be the smallest element at which an increasing subsequence of length lll ends.

Initially we assume d[0]=−∞d[0] = -\inftyd[0]=−∞ and for all other lengths d[l]=∞d[l] = \inftyd[l]=∞.

We will again gradually process the numbers, first a[0]a[0]a[0], then a[1]a[1]a[1], etc, and in each step maintain the array d[]d[]d[] so that it is up to date.

example

Given the array a={8,3,4,6,5,2,0,7,9,1}a = \{8, 3, 4, 6, 5, 2, 0, 7, 9, 1\}a={8,3,4,6,5,2,0,7,9,1}, here are all their prefixes and their dynamic programming array. Notice, that the values of the array don't always change at the end.

prefix={}d={−∞,∞,… }prefix={8}d={−∞,8,∞,… }prefix={8,3}d={−∞,3,∞,… }prefix={8,3,4}d={−∞,3,4,∞,… }prefix={8,3,4,6}d={−∞,3,4,6,∞,… }prefix={8,3,4,6,5}d={−∞,3,4,5,∞,… }prefix={8,3,4,6,5,2}d={−∞,2,4,5,∞,… }prefix={8,3,4,6,5,2,0}d={−∞,0,4,5,∞,… }prefix={8,3,4,6,5,2,0,7}d={−∞,0,4,5,7,∞,… }prefix={8,3,4,6,5,2,0,7,9}d={−∞,0,4,5,7,9,∞,… }prefix={8,3,4,6,5,2,0,7,9,1}d={−∞,0,1,5,7,9,∞,… }\begin{array}{ll} \text{prefix} = \{\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, \infty, \dots\}\\ \text{prefix} = \{8\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, 8, \infty, \dots\}\\ \text{prefix} = \{8, 3\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, 3, \infty, \dots\}\\ \text{prefix} = \{8, 3, 4\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, 3, 4, \infty, \dots\}\\ \text{prefix} = \{8, 3, 4, 6\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, 3, 4, 6, \infty, \dots\}\\ \text{prefix} = \{8, 3, 4, 6, 5\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, 3, 4, 5, \infty, \dots\}\\ \text{prefix} = \{8, 3, 4, 6, 5, 2\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, 2, 4, 5, \infty, \dots \}\\ \text{prefix} = \{8, 3, 4, 6, 5, 2, 0\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, 0, 4, 5, \infty, \dots \}\\ \text{prefix} = \{8, 3, 4, 6, 5, 2, 0, 7\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, 0, 4, 5, 7, \infty, \dots \}\\ \text{prefix} = \{8, 3, 4, 6, 5, 2, 0, 7, 9\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, 0, 4, 5, 7, 9, \infty, \dots \}\\ \text{prefix} = \{8, 3, 4, 6, 5, 2, 0, 7, 9, 1\} &\quad d = \{-\infty, 0, 1, 5, 7, 9, \infty, \dots \}\\ \end{array}prefix={}prefix={8}prefix={8,3}prefix={8,3,4}prefix={8,3,4,6}prefix={8,3,4,6,5}prefix={8,3,4,6,5,2}prefix={8,3,4,6,5,2,0}prefix={8,3,4,6,5,2,0,7}prefix={8,3,4,6,5,2,0,7,9}prefix={8,3,4,6,5,2,0,7,9,1}​d={−∞,∞,…}d={−∞,8,∞,…}d={−∞,3,∞,…}d={−∞,3,4,∞,…}d={−∞,3,4,6,∞,…}d={−∞,3,4,5,∞,…}d={−∞,2,4,5,∞,…}d={−∞,0,4,5,∞,…}d={−∞,0,4,5,7,∞,…}d={−∞,0,4,5,7,9,∞,…}d={−∞,0,1,5,7,9,∞,…}​

When we process a[i]a[i]a[i], we can ask ourselves. What have the conditions to be, that we write the current number a[i]a[i]a[i] into the d[0…n]d[0 \dots n]d[0…n] array?

We set d[l]=a[i]d[l] = a[i]d[l]=a[i], if there is a longest increasing sequence of length lll that ends in a[i]a[i]a[i], and there is no longest increasing sequence of length lll that ends in a smaller number. Similar to the previous approach, if we remove the number a[i]a[i]a[i] from the longest increasing sequence of length lll, we get another longest increasing sequence of length l−1l -1l−1. So we want to extend a longest increasing sequence of length l−1l - 1l−1 by the number a[i]a[i]a[i], and obviously the longest increasing sequence of length l−1l - 1l−1 that ends with the smallest element will work the best, in other words the sequence of length l−1l-1l−1 that ends in element d[l−1]d[l-1]d[l−1].

There is a longest increasing sequence of length l−1l - 1l−1 that we can extend with the number a[i]a[i]a[i], exactly if d[l−1]<a[i]d[l-1] < a[i]d[l−1]<a[i]. So we can just iterate over each length lll, and check if we can extend a longest increasing sequence of length l−1l - 1l−1 by checking the criteria.

Additionally we also need to check, if we maybe have already found a longest increasing sequence of length lll with a smaller number at the end. So we only update if a[i]<d[l]a[i] < d[l]a[i]<d[l].

After processing all the elements of a[]a[]a[] the length of the desired subsequence is the largest lll with d[l]<∞d[l] < \inftyd[l]<∞.

The ±∞\pm\infty±∞ padding is only a convenience for stating the recurrence; it never has to be stored. In the implementations below we keep just the entries for lengths that have actually been achieved. Then d[]d[]d[] grows by at most one element per step, reaching a position past its end is what d[l]=∞d[l] = \inftyd[l]=∞ stood for, and the answer is simply its size.

int lis(vector<int> const& a) {
    vector<int> d;
    for (int x : a) {
        size_t l = 0;
        while (l < d.size() && d[l] < x)
            l++;
        if (l == d.size())
            d.push_back(x);
        else
            d[l] = x;
    }
    return d.size();
}

We now make two important observations.

  1. The array ddd will always be sorted: d[l−1]<d[l]d[l-1] < d[l]d[l−1]<d[l] for all l=1…nl = 1 \dots nl=1…n.

    This is trivial, as you can just remove the last element from the increasing subsequence of length lll, and you get a increasing subsequence of length l−1l-1l−1 with a smaller ending number.

  2. The element a[i]a[i]a[i] will only update at most one value d[l]d[l]d[l].

    This follows immediately from the above implementation. There can only be one place in the array with d[l−1]<a[i]<d[l]d[l-1] < a[i] < d[l]d[l−1]<a[i]<d[l].

Thus we can find this element in the array d[]d[]d[] using binary search in O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn). In fact we can simply look in the array d[]d[]d[] for the first number that is strictly greater than a[i]a[i]a[i], and we try to update this element in the same way as the above implementation.

Implementation

This gives us the improved O(nlog⁡n)O(n \log n)O(nlogn) implementation, which differs from the one above only in how the position is found:

int lis(vector<int> const& a) {
    vector<int> d;
    for (int x : a) {
        auto it = lower_bound(d.begin(), d.end(), x);
        if (it == d.end())
            d.push_back(x);
        else
            *it = x;
    }
    return d.size();
}

Restoring the subsequence

It is also possible to restore the subsequence using this approach. A straightforward way is to maintain two auxiliary arrays: one mapping each position of d[]d[]d[] back to its index in a[]a[]a[], and an array of "ancestors" p[i]p[i]p[i] holding the index of the previous element of the optimal subsequence ending in a[i]a[i]a[i].

However, we can restore the subsequence in a more memory-efficient way, using only a single auxiliary array p[0…n−1]p[0 \dots n-1]p[0…n−1], recorded as a by-product of the binary search that the algorithm already performs. We let p[i]p[i]p[i] be the position in d[]d[]d[] at which a[i]a[i]a[i] ends up, so that the longest increasing subsequence ending in a[i]a[i]a[i] has length p[i]+1p[i] + 1p[i]+1.

Now suppose the length of the LIS is LLL, and let us iterate over a[]a[]a[] backwards, picking the last element with p[i]=L−1p[i] = L - 1p[i]=L−1, then the last element before it with p[i]=L−2p[i] = L - 2p[i]=L−2, and so on down to p[i]=0p[i] = 0p[i]=0. Every element picked this way is a valid predecessor of the previously picked one. Indeed, suppose we have already picked a[j]a[j]a[j] with p[j]=l+1p[j] = l + 1p[j]=l+1, and let a[i]a[i]a[i] be the last element before it with p[i]=lp[i] = lp[i]=l. Since d[l]d[l]d[l] always holds the most recent element placed at position lll, it was equal to a[i]a[i]a[i] at the moment a[j]a[j]a[j] was processed. And the binary search placed a[j]a[j]a[j] at position l+1l + 1l+1 exactly because d[l]<a[j]d[l] < a[j]d[l]<a[j], therefore a[i]<a[j]a[i] < a[j]a[i]<a[j].

Collecting the elements this way and reversing them at the end gives us a longest increasing subsequence.

vector<int> lis(vector<int> const& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    vector<int> d, p(n);

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        auto it = lower_bound(d.begin(), d.end(), a[i]);
        p[i] = it - d.begin();
        if (it == d.end())
            d.push_back(a[i]);
        else
            *it = a[i];
    }

    int l = d.size() - 1;
    vector<int> subseq;
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0 && l >= 0; i--) {
        if (p[i] == l) {
            subseq.push_back(a[i]);
            l--;
        }
    }
    reverse(subseq.begin(), subseq.end());
    return subseq;
}

Solution in O(nlog⁡n)O(n \log n)O(nlogn) with data structures {data-toc-label="Solution in O(n log n) with data structures"}

Instead of the above method for computing the longest increasing subsequence in O(nlog⁡n)O(n \log n)O(nlogn) we can also solve the problem in a different way: using some simple data structures.

Let's go back to the first method. Remember that d[i]d[i]d[i] is the value d[j]+1d[j] + 1d[j]+1 with j<ij < ij<i and a[j]<a[i]a[j] < a[i]a[j]<a[i].

Thus if we define an additional array t[]t[]t[] such that

t[a[i]]=d[i],t[a[i]] = d[i],t[a[i]]=d[i],

then the problem of computing the value d[i]d[i]d[i] is equivalent to finding the maximum value in a prefix of the array t[]t[]t[]:

d[i]=max⁡(t[0…a[i]−1]+1)d[i] = \max\left(t[0 \dots a[i] - 1] + 1\right)d[i]=max(t[0…a[i]−1]+1)

The problem of finding the maximum of a prefix of an array (which changes) is a standard problem that can be solved by many different data structures. For instance we can use a Segment tree or a Fenwick tree.

This method has obviously some shortcomings: in terms of length and complexity of the implementation this approach will be worse than the method using binary search. In addition if the input numbers a[i]a[i]a[i] are especially large, then we would have to use some tricks, like compressing the numbers (i.e. renumber them from 000 to n−1n-1n−1), or use a dynamic segment tree (only generate the branches of the tree that are important). Otherwise the memory consumption will be too high.

On the other hand this method has also some advantages: with this method you don't have to think about any tricky properties in the dynamic programming solution. And this approach allows us to generalize the problem very easily (see below).

Related tasks

Here are several problems that are closely related to the problem of finding the longest increasing subsequence.

Longest non-decreasing subsequence

This is in fact nearly the same problem. Only now it is allowed to use identical numbers in the subsequence.

The solution is essentially also nearly the same. We just have to change the inequality signs, and make a slight modification to the binary search.

Number of longest increasing subsequences

We can use the first discussed method, either the O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) version or the version using data structures. We only have to additionally store in how many ways we can obtain longest increasing subsequences ending in the values d[i]d[i]d[i].

The number of ways to form a longest increasing subsequences ending in a[i]a[i]a[i] is the sum of all ways for all longest increasing subsequences ending in jjj where d[j]d[j]d[j] is maximal. There can be multiple such jjj, so we need to sum all of them.

Using a Segment tree this approach can also be implemented in O(nlog⁡n)O(n \log n)O(nlogn).

It is not possible to use the binary search approach for this task.

Smallest number of non-increasing subsequences covering a sequence

For a given array with nnn numbers a[0…n−1]a[0 \dots n - 1]a[0…n−1] we have to colorize the numbers in the smallest number of colors, so that each color forms a non-increasing subsequence.

To solve this, we notice that the minimum number of required colors is equal to the length of the longest increasing subsequence.

Proof: We need to prove the duality of these two problems.

Let's denote by xxx the length of the longest increasing subsequence and by yyy the least number of non-increasing subsequences that form a cover. We need to prove that x=yx = yx=y.

It is clear that y<xy < xy<x is not possible, because if we have xxx strictly increasing elements, than no two can be part of the same non-increasing subsequence. Therefore we have y≥xy \ge xy≥x.

We now show that y>xy > xy>x is not possible by contradiction. Suppose that y>xy > xy>x. Then we consider any optimal set of yyy non-increasing subsequences. We transform this in set in the following way: as long as there are two such subsequences such that the first begins before the second subsequence, and the first sequence start with a number greater than or equal to the second, then we unhook this starting number and attach it to the beginning of second. After a finite number of steps we have yyy subsequences, and their starting numbers will form an increasing subsequence of length yyy. Since we assumed that y>xy > xy>x we reached a contradiction.

Thus it follows that y=xy = xy=x.

Restoring the sequences: The desired partition of the sequence into subsequences can be done greedily. I.e. go from left to right and assign the current number or that subsequence ending with the minimal number which is greater than or equal to the current one.
